The Idea

Council Decisions, Explained Before the Vote

Municipal councils make decisions about housing, transit, public safety, parks, and other local services. The source material is public, but it can be difficult to find and interpret. Deme presents upcoming agenda items in plain language, lets residents weigh in before decisions are made, and preserves recorded votes for review. It’s about bringing back the roots of democracy — starting with the local ward.

Decisions That Affect Daily LifeCity Council regularly considers housing, transit, public safety, parks, and other local services.
Limited Routine CoverageMany municipal agenda items receive limited day-to-day media coverage.
Complex Public RecordsAgendas and recorded vote data are published across documents and data files that may require time to interpret.
Individual Records VaryA councillor-by-councillor breakdown is available only when a recorded vote is requested.

Trust Is the Product

Neutral, Private, and Free by Design

Strictly non-partisan

Deme is strictly non-partisan — our briefs explain what each vote would do, never how to vote. Editorial standards are set before launch. Every brief identifies its sources and follows a neutral-language checklist. No party, campaign, or donor determines coverage.

Private by Default

Signing up asks for your email and postal code; no full address or name is required. You control what you share, and your positions are not sold or shared.

Clear About the Numbers

When Deme launches, results will be labelled “verified users in this ward” and will not be presented as representative of the entire public. When participation is low, Deme will show response counts rather than percentages.

Free to Use

Deme is an independent civic-tech project. Users are not charged to participate.

“A public record that makes council decisions easier to find, understand, and compare.”
Transparency

Where Our Data Comes From

The Record is built from the City of Toronto’s official council vote records and the City’s council agenda system (TMMIS). We keep the source material separate from our plain-language explanations.

Official Records

Agenda items retain the published title, date, council or committee, and subject topics. When a councillor-by-councillor recorded vote is available, we show each councillor’s vote.

Coverage

Career recorded vote totals span 2006–2026. Row-level recorded vote details cover the 2018–2026 term; searchable agenda items in this snapshot cover 2018–2026.

Refreshed in October 2026

This is a fixed public-record snapshot, not a live City feed. New or corrected City records appear only after the dataset is refreshed.

Briefs Explain, Not Persuade

Plain-language briefs summarize the official agenda text. They provide neutral explanations rather than Deme editorial positions.

Why Many Agenda Items Have No Recorded Vote to Show:

A councillor-by-councillor breakdown is available only when a recorded vote is requested. Other agenda items may be decided without that breakdown, received for information, or presented without a decision. In this snapshot, 3,162 of 33,775 agenda items have individual councillor votes.

Corrections

When we correct an error in a brief or a record, we note it here with a timestamp.

  • October 6, 2026 — No corrections yet. Last reviewed October 6, 2026.

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Deme?

Deme (pronounced “deem,” like “team”) is named after the deme — the local ward of ancient Athens, where everyday people took part in running their city. It’s the root of the word democracy. Our goal is simple: make sure you know what’s being voted on before your representatives vote, explained in plain language — so you can weigh in while it still counts, and see exactly how each of them voted after.

Words we use
Carried
The motion passed — more councillors voted yes than no.
Lost
The motion did not pass — more councillors voted no than yes.
Decided
The motion has been decided — the outcome is final.
Amendment
A proposed change to the wording of a motion. Council votes on amendments before taking the main vote.
Documented
We found this promise stated in the candidate’s own campaign materials.
Source linked
There’s a link to the original document so you can check it yourself.
Vote-linked
This promise is connected to real council votes on the topic, so you can see what actually happened.
Absent
The councillor was not recorded as voting on this motion.
Interest declared
The councillor declared a conflict of interest and did not vote, as the rules require.
Is Deme free?

Yes. Deme is an independent civic-tech project, and there is no charge to participate.

Does Deme take sides?

No. Deme is strictly non-partisan — our briefs explain what each vote would do, never how to vote. Every brief identifies its sources and follows a neutral-language checklist, and corrections are noted with a timestamp. No party, campaign, or donor determines coverage.

How are the plain-language briefs written?

Every brief is an original plain-language summary written from the official City of Toronto agenda record for that item — the published title, the meeting it belonged to, and the recorded outcome. Briefs describe what a vote would do; they never tell you how to vote.

Figures in a brief come only from the official record. We never invent numbers, and we never round figures into new ones.

Neutral-language checklist (draft):

  • Describe what the vote would do, not whether it is good or bad.
  • Use everyday words; explain jargon the first time it appears.
  • Include only figures that appear in the official record.
  • Name the mover, seconder, and decision body factually.
  • No adjectives that praise or blame — no cheerleading, no alarm.
  • Say plainly what is unknown or undecided.
How fresh is the data?

This site is a fixed public-record snapshot, not a live City feed. We rebuild it from the City of Toronto’s official records each time we publish an update, and the snapshot date is always shown here.

Snapshot changelog:

  • October 6, 2026 — Full refresh: 33,775 searchable agenda items (2018–2026); 3,162 items with councillor-by-councillor recorded vote splits; 33,775 plain-language briefs.
What do I get when I join?

Before a vote, you receive a 30-second plain-language brief explaining the agenda item, the proposed change, and who may be affected. You can then select Support or Oppose so your response is included in your ward’s totals. After the decision, you receive the result and your representatives’ recorded votes. The proposed limit is one alert per day, with none sent after 9 p.m.

What do you collect about me?

The waitlist asks for your email and postal code, which are used to notify you at launch and match you with your representatives. No full address or name is required.

Will it cover more than Toronto?

Deme is designed to cover municipal, provincial, and federal governments. The pilot starts with Toronto City Council.

When can I start using it?

The Toronto pilot is in development, and the waitlist is open. Join the waitlist to be notified when you can receive alerts and weigh in on upcoming votes in your area.
